prompt:
Prompt v1 (answer line written as SMILES: <smiles>), 50 images:

You are reading one chemical structure image and writing down the molecule it depicts, as SMILES.

This is a blind test: read the structure from the drawing itself.

Guidance:
- Look at the image carefully, region by region. Count ring vertices and chain carbons one at a time, and check every heteroatom label, charge and bond order.
- Include stereochemistry (@/@@, /, \) only where the drawing actually shows wedges/hashes or cis/trans geometry. A carbon that is a stereocentre by connectivity but is drawn with plain bonds gets no stereo.
- Expand any abbreviation you can read (Me, Et, Ph, Boc, Ac, OMe, Ts, Bn, CF3, NHAc, etc.) into explicit atoms.
- Before answering, check that your SMILES is valid and that it describes the drawing atom for atom.
- Give one answer even if you are not certain of it.

End your response with exactly one line of this form, with nothing after it:
SMILES: <smiles>

Prompt v2 (answer line shown as SMILES: CCO), 235 images:

You are reading one chemical structure image and writing down the molecule it depicts, as SMILES.

This is a blind test: read the structure from the drawing itself.

Guidance:
- Look at the image carefully, region by region. Count ring vertices and chain carbons one at a time, and check every heteroatom label, charge and bond order.
- Include stereochemistry (@/@@, /, \) only where the drawing actually shows wedges/hashes or cis/trans geometry. A carbon that is a stereocentre by connectivity but is drawn with plain bonds gets no stereo.
- Expand any abbreviation you can read (Me, Et, Ph, Boc, Ac, OMe, Ts, Bn, CF3, NHAc, etc.) into explicit atoms.
- Before answering, check that your SMILES is valid and that it describes the drawing atom for atom.
- Give one answer even if you are not certain of it.

End your response with exactly one line that starts with "SMILES: " followed by the bare SMILES string, with nothing after it. For example, for ethanol the last line would be:
SMILES: CCO

points: Sonnet 5.5 (claude-sonnet-5-5) reading the first 285 corpus images in manifest order, one Messages API call per image: the PNG as base64 and a fixed prompt (below). No tools, no code, no second look, no shared context between images.

The answer is the last "SMILES: ..." line of the reply. Adaptive thinking at the API default. Output budget: max_tokens 16,000 for the first rows, 64,000 (streamed) from the switch on; each row records its own.

A reading that runs out of output is retried and scored on the retry, flagged on its tile (↻) and in its sheet: a row read at 16,000 is re-read once at 64,000; one that runs out at 64,000 gets one retry with an added instruction to commit to an answer after one careful pass. Both attempts are kept and counted in the cost.
Scored exactly like the other Sonnet tabs: RDKit canonical SMILES against the PubChem reference, exact / stereo-only / wrong / unparseable.
The Sonnet 5.5 tab's reader is an agent: it crops, runs RDKit, re-renders its answer and diffs it against the image. Compared here only on the images both have read.

headline: One API call per image, no tools. Cost at Sonnet 5.5 list price ($2 / $10 per MTok). 4 prompt-v1 answers came wrapped in <smiles> tags and were unwrapped before scoring.
footer: n=285, the first 285 corpus images in manifest order. Prompt versions: Prompt v1 (answer line written as SMILES: <smiles>): 50 images, 98.0% exact; Prompt v2 (answer line shown as SMILES: CCO): 235 images, 93.2% exact. Output budget per first attempt: max_tokens 16,000: 185 images; max_tokens 64,000: 100 images; 1 max_tokens rows retried, 1 finished, 1 exact. Exact 268/285; stereo only 15; wrong 2; unparseable or no SMILES line 0 (no SMILES line: 0). Stop reasons other than end_turn: max_tokens 1. $5.66 in total. 4 replies wrote the answer as <smiles>...</smiles> (the prompt's placeholder taken literally); the tags are stripped before scoring, which moves 4 from unparseable to exact. Ground truth is PubChem.
